screens.title: Python and SQLite: Connecting and Creating Tables
screens.narratorSegment: Today you'll learn how Python talks to SQLite files. The sqlite3 module is part of Python's standard library, so you can start without extra installs. We'll open or create a database file, make a cursor that sends S Q L commands, and define table schemas with CREATE TABLE. You'll also learn the habit of committing changes and closing connections, and how to protect your script with error handling so a file permission error or S Q L syntax issue won't crash your program. For example, running sqlite3. connect with a filename will create that file if it doesn't exist, letting you programmatically build databases during development. As you follow the examples, notice the patterns you will reuse: obtain a connection, create a cursor, execute S Q L, commit changes, and close the connection in a finally block. These steps keep your data safe and your code predictable. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to create Users, Products, and related Customers and Orders tables from Python with confidence. Think about one application you might store locally as a single file and we will make that possible.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical abilities that prepare you to manage local application data. First, you'll understand the sqlite3 module: what it provides and why it is included in the Python standard library. Knowing this helps you choose the right tool when you need a single-file, transactional database. Second, you'll be able to open a connection to a database file using sqlite3. connect and recognize that this call creates the file if it does not exist. That knowledge helps you programmatically manage databases without manual setup. Third, you'll create a cursor object and use it to execute S Q L statements and fetch results. The cursor is the interface between Python and S Q L. Fourth, you'll write and run CREATE TABLE statements from Python and use the IF NOT EXISTS clause to make those operations idempotent during repeated runs. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or pattern you can reuse daily, and successful completion means you've achieved verified competency toward building simple local databases.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Robust Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Alongside the basic workflow, you will learn four robust practices that prevent common failures. First, implement try, except, and finally blocks around database operations so your script can catch sqlite3. Error exceptions and still close the connection cleanly. This avoids leaving the database locked or in an inconsistent state. Second, make committing explicit: call conn. commit after schema or data changes so the file is actually updated on disk. Forgetting commit is a frequent source of confusion. Third, use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS to make table creation idempotent during development and repeated runs. That reduces noisy errors when you re-run setup scripts. Fourth, design table columns with sensible constraints and defaults, such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and DEFAULT values, to protect data integrity at the schema level. Together these practices make your scripts predictable and maintainable when creating and evolving local databases.

screens.title: sqlite3 module and SQLite fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: sqlite3 is the built-in Python module that gives you a straightforward A P I to work with SQLite databases. SQLite itself is a serverless, self-contained, zero-configuration, transactional S Q L engine that stores an entire database in a single file. This matters because you can bundle an application with a database file, move it between machines, and avoid the overhead of installing and managing a separate database server. A concrete example: a small inventory tracker app can store all data in products. db and be shared as a single file. A common misconception is thinking SQLite is only for toy projects; while it's not a drop-in replacement for high-scale client-server databases, it is production-ready for many small-to-medium workloads and for local caches and tests. Key properties to remember are transactional safety, file-based storage, and S Q L compatibility. Takeaway: sqlite3 gives you Python-native access to a single-file S Q L database, making it ideal for development, local tools, and simple applications. Question: what properties of your app would make SQLite an appropriate choice? sqlite3 module and SQLite fundamentals means built-in module that exposes sqlite functionality to python scripts for file-based, transactional databases.. In practical terms, what sqlite3 provides and why sqlite is a good local database. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › What is sqlite3?
sqlite3 module

A compact API included with Python that lets you open and operate on SQLite database files using standard SQL.

Core property
Serverless single-file storage with ACID transactions.
Concrete example
A desktop notes app keeping all records in notes.db for simple distribution and backup.
Misconception
It is not only for learning; it can be reliable for many production scenarios that suit single-file storage.
Key Takeaway

sqlite3 makes it easy to use SQL in Python without external servers; pick SQLite when you need a lightweight, transactional local store.

screens.title: Open a database with sqlite3.connect()
screens.narratorSegment: Opening a connection is the first concrete step. The function sqlite3. connect takes a filename and returns a connection object. If that file does not exist, SQLite will create it for you. This behavior makes it easy to initialize application storage: simply pick a filename and your script will establish the file-based database. A common beginner pattern is to write conn = sqlite3. connect('my_first_database. db') and then proceed to create a cursor and run S Q L. A misconception to avoid is assuming connect immediately writes schemas or data; it only establishes a link and may create the file but changes are not permanent until you call commit. Example: run the code fragment shown on the screen and you will see the printed "Database connected successfully!" message when the connection opens. Finally, always consider where you place the database file in your project; choose writable paths and avoid creating files in restricted system directories. Question: what filename would you choose for a local notebook app and why? Open a database with sqlite3.connect() means sqlite3.connect(filename) opens or creates a database file and returns a connection used for all subsequent operations.. In practical terms, connect to a file; discover that it is created if missing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

import sqlite3

screens.title: Cursor object: your SQL remote control
screens.narratorSegment: After you have a connection object, the next step is to create a cursor. A cursor is a lightweight object that acts as an interface for executing S Q L commands and retrieving results. Think of it as a remote control for the database: you press execute on the cursor, and the database runs a command on your behalf. In Python, you call cursor = conn. cursor() to create it. You then use cursor. execute with an S Q L string to run commands like CREATE TABLE, INSERT, or SELECT. A practical example: create a cursor, execute a CREATE TABLE statement, and then commit. A common misconception is that connection objects execute S Q L directly; instead, the cursor is the one that sends S Q L to the engine. Also, when fetching data from SELECT queries, you call cursor. fetchone or cursor. fetchall to retrieve rows. Takeaway: cursors are the operational bridge between Python code and the S Q L engine. Ask yourself: when you query for a single record, which fetch method is most efficient and why? Cursor object: your SQL remote control means use conn.cursor() to create a cursor; call cursor.execute to send sql and cursor.fetch* to retrieve results.. In practical terms, create a cursor and use it to execute statements and fetch results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Cursor
Cursor example

Create a cursor from the connection and use it to run SQL.

cursor = conn.cursor()
print("Cursor created successfully!")

# Run a simple query
cursor.execute('SELECT name, email FROM users')
rows = cursor.fetchall()
for row in rows:
  print(row)
Note
Use fetchone for a single record to avoid loading large result sets into memory.
Why it matters

The cursor is how Python communicates SQL intent. Proper use of fetch methods keeps your app efficient and predictable.

Key Takeaway

A cursor executes SQL and returns results; choose fetchone or fetchall based on expected result size.

screens.title: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS — idempotent schema creation
screens.narratorSegment: Creating tables from Python follows the same S Q L you already know, but with a few practical considerations. Use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS to make the operation safe to run multiple times during development. In the example shown on the screen, we define a users table with an id column set as an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, a name column as TEXT NOT NULL, and an email column with UNIQUE and NOT NULL constraints. These constraints enforce essential data integrity rules at the schema level. After executing the CREATE TABLE statement with cursor. execute, you must call conn. commit to persist the schema change to disk. A common mistake is to forget commit, then look for the table in a separate tool and conclude the script failed. Another misconception is that AUTOINCREMENT is always required; INTEGER PRIMARY KEY without the AUTOINCREMENT keyword will still auto-generate unique ids in SQLite, but AUTOINCREMENT changes how ids are assigned over the long term. Takeaway: write explicit CREATE TABLE statements, protect them with IF NOT EXISTS, and remember to commit. CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS — idempotent schema creation means use create table if not exists to define schema safely and commit changes so they become permanent.. In practical terms, define columns, types, primary keys, and use if not exists to avoid errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS to define schema safely and commit changes so they become permanent.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › CREATE TABLE
Schema example

A users table with primary key and constraints to ensure valid data.

try:
    cursor.execute('''
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
            id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
            name TEXT NOT NULL,
            email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL
        )
    ''')
    print("Table 'users' created or already exists.")
    conn.commit()
except sqlite3.Error as e:
    print(f"An error occurred: {e}")
finally:
    conn.close()
    print("Database connection closed.")
Tip
IF NOT EXISTS makes setup scripts safe to run repeatedly during development and tests.
Schema notes
  • Define primary keys to uniquely identify rows.
  • Use NOT NULL and UNIQUE to prevent invalid or duplicate entries.
  • Use DEFAULT for sensible automatic values where appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Write explicit CREATE TABLE statements, protect them with IF NOT EXISTS, and commit to persist schema changes.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Users example
Complete example

This script shows the defensive pattern: initialize conn, connect, create cursor, run CREATE TABLE, commit, and close.

import sqlite3

conn = None # Initialize conn to None for error handling
try:
    conn = sqlite3.connect('my_first_database.db')
    cursor = conn.cursor()

    cursor.execute('''
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
            id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
            name TEXT NOT NULL,
            email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL
        )
    ''')
    print("Table 'users' created or already exists.")
    conn.commit()

except sqlite3.Error as e:
    print(f"An error occurred: {e}")
finally:
    if conn:
        conn.close()
        print("Database connection closed.")
Common mistake
Forgetting to initialize conn leads to errors when closing in finally if connection failed.
Practice
Run the script twice to confirm IF NOT EXISTS prevents errors on the second run.

DEFAULT constraints provide predictable values when inserts omit a column, avoiding nulls that later complicate logic. screens.title: Commit and Close — making changes permanent
screens.narratorSegment: Transactions are how changes in SQLite become permanent. When you execute a CREATE TABLE or INSERT, the change is staged in the connection's transaction. Calling conn. commit flushes those changes to disk and makes them visible to other processes and tools. Forgetting to commit is a common source of confusion: you may run a script, see no errors, and then open the database in a browser and find the table missing. Calling conn. close releases the file lock and ensures all resources are freed. Therefore, the safe sequence is: execute your S Q L, call conn. commit to persist, and finally close the connection. A subtle misconception is believing commit is only for data manipulation; it is equally critical after schema changes. Also, closing without committing will discard uncommitted changes. Takeaway: always commit after structural or data changes and close connections to avoid locks or data loss. content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Error Handling
Try / Except / Finally pattern

Use defensive initialization and finally to close the connection regardless of errors.

import sqlite3

conn = None
try:
    conn = sqlite3.connect('ecommerce.db')
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    # execute statements
    conn.commit()
except sqlite3.Error as e:
    print(f"Database error: {e}")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"General error: {e}")
finally:
    if conn:
        conn.close()
        print("Database connection closed.")
Tip
Initialize conn to None so finally can safely check and close it only when set.
Common failures
  • Permission errors when creating a file in a protected path.
  • SQL syntax mistakes causing sqlite3.Error exceptions.
  • Uncommitted changes lost when not calling commit.
Key Takeaway

Expect database operations to fail; catch sqlite3.Error and use finally to close connections to preserve integrity.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Customers & Orders
Create related tables

Define Customers and Orders; Orders references Customers.customer_id as a foreign key.

# Customers table
cursor.execute('''
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Customers (
        customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
        name TEXT NOT NULL,
        email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL
    )
''')

# Orders table with foreign key reference
cursor.execute('''
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Orders (
        order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
        customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
        order_date TEXT NOT NULL,
        total_amount REAL NOT NULL,
        FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES Customers(customer_id)
    )
''')
conn.commit()
Note
Store dates as text 'YYYY-MM-DD' for simplicity in small apps, or use integer timestamps when needed.
Schema architecture
Parent table: Customers holds identity. Child table: Orders holds transactional rows linked by customer_id. Referential integrity is expressed by the FOREIGN KEY clause.
Key Takeaway

Model relationships with primary and foreign keys so your data remains connected and queries can join related rows reliably.

fullNarratorScript:
Today you'll learn how Python talks to SQLite files. The sqlite3 module is part of Python's standard library, so you can start without extra installs. We'll open or create a database file, make a cursor that sends S Q L commands, and define table schemas with CREATE TABLE. You'll also learn the habit of committing changes and closing connections, and how to protect your script with error handling so a file permission error or S Q L syntax issue won't crash your program. For example, running sqlite3. connect with a filename will create that file if it doesn't exist, letting you programmatically build databases during development. As you follow the examples, notice the patterns you will reuse: obtain a connection, create a cursor, execute S Q L, commit changes, and close the connection in a finally block. These steps keep your data safe and your code predictable. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to create Users, Products, and related Customers and Orders tables from Python with confidence. Think about one application you might store locally as a single file and we will make that possible.

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical abilities that prepare you to manage local application data. First, you'll understand the sqlite3 module: what it provides and why it is included in the Python standard library. Knowing this helps you choose the right tool when you need a single-file, transactional database. Second, you'll be able to open a connection to a database file using sqlite3. connect and recognize that this call creates the file if it does not exist. That knowledge helps you programmatically manage databases without manual setup. Third, you'll create a cursor object and use it to execute S Q L statements and fetch results. The cursor is the interface between Python and S Q L. Fourth, you'll write and run CREATE TABLE statements from Python and use the IF NOT EXISTS clause to make those operations idempotent during repeated runs. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or pattern you can reuse daily, and successful completion means you've achieved verified competency toward building simple local databases.

Alongside the basic workflow, you will learn four robust practices that prevent common failures. First, implement try, except, and finally blocks around database operations so your script can catch sqlite3. Error exceptions and still close the connection cleanly. This avoids leaving the database locked or in an inconsistent state. Second, make committing explicit: call conn. commit after schema or data changes so the file is actually updated on disk. Forgetting commit is a frequent source of confusion. Third, use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS to make table creation idempotent during development and repeated runs. That reduces noisy errors when you re-run setup scripts. Fourth, design table columns with sensible constraints and defaults, such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and DEFAULT values, to protect data integrity at the schema level. Together these practices make your scripts predictable and maintainable when creating and evolving local databases.

sqlite3 is the built-in Python module that gives you a straightforward A P I to work with SQLite databases. SQLite itself is a serverless, self-contained, zero-configuration, transactional S Q L engine that stores an entire database in a single file. This matters because you can bundle an application with a database file, move it between machines, and avoid the overhead of installing and managing a separate database server. A concrete example: a small inventory tracker app can store all data in products. db and be shared as a single file.
